claims.text: A combined atomistic-simulation and Boltzmann-transport approach can separately predict lattice and electronic thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed approach will have significantly lower error than earlier analytical estimates that conflate lattice and electronic transport.
The target material is defect-free, near-equiatomic, bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
DFT-derived elastic and vibrational properties, with a temperature-dependent Debye temperature, will be used to calculate lattice thermal conductivity.
Electronic-structure calculations and Boltzmann transport theory will be used separately to calculate electronic thermal conductivity.
Electronic and lattice thermal-conductivity contributions become comparable below 200 K.
Configurational disorder in HfNbTaTiZr causes phonon scattering.
The effects of configurational disorder and phonon scattering can be captured through DFT-derived vibrational densities of states and elastic tensors.
Applying a single Debye temperature to a composite lattice-plus-electronic conduction model introduces error.
Separately modeling lattice and electronic transport avoids the error associated with a single-Debye-temperature composite model.
Calculated electronic scattering rates and transport coefficients can independently determine the electronic thermal-conductivity contribution.
Predicted lattice thermal conductivity will agree with experiment within ±10% from 300 to 1200 K.
The predicted electronic contribution will be consistent with separated low-temperature measurements below 200 K.
The proposed method will reduce combined prediction error by approximately 15–20% relative to earlier analytical methods.
Earlier models represented HfNbTaTiZr as a perfect, defect-free bulk crystal.
Earlier models used a single Debye parameter or simplified estimates that conflated lattice and electronic thermal transport.
The proposed approach is applicable to high-purity, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr over 100–1200 K.
Significant oxygen contamination or other defects will reduce the accuracy of the proposed approach.
Accuracy will diminish at temperatures well outside 100–1200 K.
Uncertainty in the error improvement and boundary-temperature decoupling efficacy is approximately ±5% because of sample-quality variation and measurement challenges.
